drafted.title: Insufficient validation of tool/agent input enabling injection and bypass
drafted.description: Agent frameworks, MCP servers, and model-serving/inference endpoints frequently accept tool-call parameters, file paths, protocol fields, or inference request values without enforcing type, range, schema, or allowlist constraints, letting an attacker supply crafted inputs (oversized tensors/tokens, path traversal strings, malformed parameter overrides, out-of-bounds ids, crafted prefixes) that cross a trust boundary unchecked. Because agents chain tool outputs into further execution, the unvalidated value typically reaches a parser, shell, deserializer, or privileged code path, resulting in remote code execution, denial of service, authentication/allowlist bypass, or sandbox/container escape.

drafted.title: External entity injection via unhardened XML parsing of tool/document input
drafted.description: An agent or a tool/library it invokes (document ingestion, SAML/SOAP handlers, spreadsheet/PDF/SVG parsers, BOM/report generators, etc.) parses attacker-supplied XML with a default XML parser that resolves DOCTYPE and external entity declarations, letting the attacker-controlled entity fetch local files or internal URLs during parsing. Because agents routinely auto-ingest untrusted documents, API responses, and tool outputs as XML without sandboxing the parser, this gives attackers a reliable path to exfiltrate local files/credentials, pivot via SSRF into internal services the agent can reach, or exhaust memory/CPU through entity-expansion (billion laughs) denial of service.

drafted.title: Unsanitized construction of downstream commands or queries from agent-controlled input
drafted.description: Agent frameworks and MCP-exposed tools build shell commands, SQL/Cypher queries, templates, or other downstream-interpreter input directly from LLM-generated or externally-influenced content (user prompts, retrieved documents, tool responses) without neutralizing special characters or delimiters. Because the agent's tool-calling layer treats this content as trusted, an attacker who can influence any upstream text gets their payload parsed as executable syntax by the downstream shell, database, template engine, or interpreter, yielding remote code execution, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation.

drafted.title: Open redirect via unvalidated redirect-target parameter
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent service accepts an attacker-controlled destination (a redirect_uri, return_to/next parameter, or Host header) and redirects, emails, or issues authorization callbacks to it without validating it against an allow-list of trusted origins. In MCP/OAuth-driven agent flows this lets an attacker craft a trusted-looking link that silently diverts the login, consent, or token-issuance step to an attacker-controlled domain, enabling OAuth code/token theft, password-reset link poisoning, or phishing that masquerades as the legitimate agent platform.

drafted.title: Path traversal via unsanitized file path parameters in tool endpoints
drafted.description: Agent-adjacent tools (model servers, web UIs, MCP-adjacent file/log/backup/extension endpoints) accept a filename or path argument from a tool call and splice it onto a base directory without canonicalizing or bounding it, so '../'-style or absolute-path sequences (including nested variants reachable via archive extraction, i.e. tar-slip) let an attacker escape the intended directory. Because an agent often forwards user- or model-controlled strings directly into these parameters, the result is arbitrary file read, write, or overwrite of sensitive paths, frequently escalating to full remote code execution.

drafted.title: Cross-origin tool invocation via missing Origin/Host validation on local MCP transport
drafted.description: An MCP server's HTTP/SSE transport accepts requests without validating the Origin or Host header (or uses a weak prefix/startswith match), so a malicious web page loaded in the victim's browser—or an attacker using DNS rebinding to resolve a domain to 127.0.0.1—can issue cross-origin requests that the locally-bound server treats as trusted, invoking privileged tools, exfiltrating data, or executing agent actions with no authentication. This breaks the implicit trust boundary that 'localhost-only' MCP servers rely on for security, turning any user who merely visits an attacker-controlled page into an unwitting proxy for full tool access.

drafted.title: Arbitrary code execution via eval injection in agent expression/code-execution engines
drafted.description: Agent frameworks, workflow builders, and tool-call parsers frequently pass user-, model-, or workflow-supplied strings (custom code nodes, expression languages, SCXML data fields, tool-call argument parsing) directly into eval()/exec()-style dynamic code evaluation without neutralizing special elements or enforcing a real sandbox boundary. An attacker who controls that string — via a crafted prompt, workflow definition, or tool-call payload — achieves arbitrary code execution in the host process, escaping the intended sandbox and compromising the entire agent runtime and any credentials or tools it holds.

drafted.title: Arbitrary file read/write via relative path traversal in agent tool file endpoints
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent tool server (e.g. MLflow, model-inference backends, chat/workflow UIs, MCP file connectors) accepts a filename or path parameter for upload, save/load, delete, or profile operations and concatenates it into a filesystem path without canonicalizing or allow-listing it, so an attacker-supplied value containing '../' sequences escapes the intended storage directory. This lets an attacker or a manipulated agent read, overwrite, or delete arbitrary files on the host — leaking secrets/config, corrupting models or run artifacts, or planting files that achieve remote code execution.

drafted.title: Unrestricted upload of dangerous file types via agent file-handling endpoints
drafted.description: AI chat/agent platforms commonly expose file-upload features (avatars, document ingestion for RAG, attachments, media galleries, config imports) that fail to validate file extension, MIME type, or content against execution context, letting an attacker upload a web shell, script, or executable config that the host server later interprets or runs. Because the agent's runtime and the upload-handling service typically share a filesystem and execution environment, this converts a routine content-ingestion feature into full remote code execution on the host running the agent.

drafted.title: Object prototype pollution via unguarded merge enabling sandbox escape
drafted.description: An attacker crafts tool/workflow input (JSON bodies, form data, template expressions, glob/path strings) containing `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype` keys that a JS-based agent runtime, workflow engine, or sandbox recursively merges or path-assigns without blocking prototype keys, corrupting Object.prototype process-wide. Because many agent frameworks reuse that polluted global state for validation, config defaults, or expression/VM sandbox construction, the attacker can bypass authz checks, hijack downstream library gadgets (HTTP clients, template/glob/parser libs), or escape the code-execution sandbox entirely to achieve arbitrary code execution.
